newsitem.title: USA: Millon Air scrambles after Ecuador crash.
newsitem.headline: Millon Air scrambles after Ecuador crash.

text.p: Millon Air, grounded following a crash last week in Ecuador, was scrambling to find other lift for its cargo during the busiest season at Miami International Airport(MIA), local cargo executives said late on Tuesday.
"They have come to us and we are looking into what we can do for them," said Jon Batchelor, senior vice president at all-cargo Arrow Air Inc. "But we are really tight right now," he said.
No comment was available from Millon as repeated calls were not returned.

Late Thursday the Federal Aviation Administration asked Millon Air to voluntarily suspend operations following the October 22 crash of Millon's 29-year-old Boeing 707 into a crowded neighborhood in Manta, Ecuador. The three crew members and 25 people on the ground were killed and at least 60 injured, some badly burned.
"I understand they have quite a bit of freight sitting around," said one executive at a rival airline.
"I'm sure we will get a lot of cargo from their customers," said B.F. Spohrer, president of Challenge Air Cargo Inc., Miami. Spohrer said he called and offered assistance to beleaguered Millon.

Executives said Millon had several options. It could temporarily lease aircraft, as long as Million employees were not involved in the flight. Or it could charter individual flights or try to find space on other carriers, which was the most likely.

Millon had only a 3.6 percent market share of international freight handled through MIA last year, according to Dade County Aviation Department. But even with its relatively small size, making alternative arrangements might not be easy.
November is the busiest month at the airport, according to MIA cargo officials.

Normally heavy southbound freight is boosted by Latin American retailers stocking up for Christmas. Flowers, fruits and vegetables travel northbound as wintry North America and Europe can no longer grow their own produce. Passenger carriers have little to no belly space due to heavier passenger demands.
For example, Amerijet International Inc. of Fort Lauderdale, has no charter or leases available of its aircraft until February, said Pam Rollins, vice president.
